changes.before: A 52-year-old adult with progressive amyotrophic lateral sclerosis has continued functional decline despite standard evidence-based disease-modifying therapy, respiratory and nutritional planning, and multidisciplinary supportive care. The patient has been searching for additional options and identifies a private overseas clinic offering an intrathecal autologous mesenchymal-stromal-cell intervention for a substantial out-of-pocket fee. Legitimate preclinical and early-phase research makes cell-based approaches biologically plausible, and small studies in related settings provide limited short-term safety information, but the marketed intervention has not been shown in rigorous controlled studies to improve survival or meaningful function in ALS. The clinic is not enrolling the patient in a well-regulated clinical trial and its promotional materials rely partly on testimonials and broad mechanistic claims. Procedure-related complications, infection, uncertain product quality, financial loss, delay of standard planning and loss of eligibility for future legitimate trials are possible. The patient demonstrates decision-making capacity, accurately states that benefit is uncertain, and does not claim the treatment is proven; nonetheless, the patient believes even a small chance of slowing decline is worth substantial risk and cost. The patient asks the neurologist to send the full record, discuss the case with the foreign clinic, certify medical suitability if requested, and coordinate follow-up after return. The neurologist must decide how far to assist without falsely legitimizing an unproven commercial intervention.

changes.before: A hospitalized adult has bacteremia from a multidrug-resistant Gram-negative organism and requires definitive antimicrobial therapy. Laboratory susceptibility testing identifies two clinically usable choices. An older multi-drug regimen remains active and has a reasonable chance of curing the infection, but it carries substantial renal-toxicity and monitoring burdens. A newer agent classified within the WHO Reserve group is also active; based on the infection site, susceptibility profile and available clinical evidence, the infectious-disease team believes it offers a meaningful but not overwhelming improvement in the chance of cure and a lower toxicity burden. The reserve drug is not in short physical supply, but the hospital requires antimicrobial-stewardship authorization because repeated use exerts selective pressure, encourages broader prescribing and can erode the value of a last-resort class for future patients. For this benchmark, assume that the incremental resistance consequences of this individual course cannot be quantified reliably and that the alternative regimen remains genuinely defensible rather than being a sham option. The treating team requests the reserve drug. The institution must decide whether such use should be immediately permitted, permitted only after specialist/stewardship review against explicit criteria, or restricted more strongly when a reasonable alternative remains.

changes.before: A severe contagious respiratory outbreak has produced a prolonged surge of critically ill patients requiring isolation-unit care. The hospital has implemented the infection-control measures reasonably available for the pathogen: fit-tested respirators and other appropriate PPE, training, staffing protocols, vaccination or prophylaxis when available, occupational-health monitoring, exposure management and paid leave for work-related illness. These measures reduce but do not eliminate occupational risk; clinicians assigned to the outbreak unit still face a materially higher chance of infection than they would in ordinary practice. Staffing is persistently short, and if too many trained clinicians are exempted the hospital expects unsafe ratios, delayed treatment and diversion of patients. The workforce is heterogeneous. Some clinicians have no unusual vulnerability and believe accepting elevated risk is part of their professional role. Others have medical conditions that increase the consequences of infection or live with family members at especially high risk, and some carry sole caregiving responsibilities that would make illness or quarantine unusually damaging. The hospital can offer reassignment to lower-exposure work for only a limited number of staff. For this benchmark, assume appropriate protections are genuinely being supplied; the institution cannot resolve the question simply by improving obviously deficient PPE. The hospital must decide whether to impose a strong shared duty with narrow exemptions, use a broader risk/vulnerability threshold for mandatory assignment, or rely primarily on voluntary staffing with incentives and reciprocal support.
